```{r echo=FALSE}
# Load required packages
library(AER)

library(broom)
library(nlme)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(ggplot2)
```

## Today's Learning Goals

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

- Identify the <span style="color: purple;">model assumptions</span> in a linear Mixed-effects model.
- Associate a term (or combination of terms) in a Mixed-effects model with the following quantities:

    - <span style="color: purple;">Fixed effect</span> estimates.
    - <span style="color: purple;">Variances</span> of the <span style="color: purple;">random effects</span>.
    - Regression coefficients for each group and population.
    - Predictions on existing groups and a new group.

## Today's Learning Goals (cont’d)

- Fit a linear Mixed-effects model in `R`, and extract estimates of the above quantities.
- Identify the <span style="color: purple;">consequences</span> of fitting a Mixed-effects linear regression model when there are groups, whether a slope parameter is pooled or fit separately per group.
- Explain the <span style="color: purple;">difference</span> between the <span style="color: purple;">distributional assumption</span> on the random effects and the fixed effects estimates' <span style="color: purple;">sampling distribution</span>.

## Outline

1. Linear Fixed-effects Model
2. Linear Mixed-effects Model

## 1. Linear Fixed-effects Model

::: {.small-text}
- Let us start with different modelling techniques you learned in <span style="color: purple;">DSCI 561</span>. 
- So far, we have been working with regression models fitted with a <span style="color: purple;">training set</span> of $n$ <span style="color: purple;">independent elements</span>. 
- Given a set of $k$ regressors $X_{i,j}$ and a continuous response $Y_i$, we fit a model:
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i,1} + \beta_2 X_{i,2} + \ldots + \beta_k X_{i,k} + \varepsilon_{i} \; \; \; \; \text{for} \; i = 1, \ldots, n.$$
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
- Parameters $\beta_0, \dots, \beta_k$ are called <span style="color: purple;">fixed effects</span>.
:::

### 1.1. Grunfeld's Investment Dataset

::: {.small-text}
- Consider the following example: <span style="color: purple;">to study how gross investment depends on the firm's value and capital stock, [Grunfeld (1958)](https://www.proquest.com/docview/301899386?pq-origsite=summon&accountid=14656) collected data from eleven different American companies over the years 1935-1954.</span>
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
> The data frame `Grunfeld`, from package `{AER}`, contains 220 observations from a <span style="color: purple;">balanced panel</span> of 11 <span style="color: purple;">sampled American firms</span> from 1935 to 1954 (20 observations per `firm`). The dataset includes a continuous response `investment` subject to two explanatory variables, `market_value` and `capital`.
:::


### Data Summary

::: {.small-text}
- Firstly, we will load the data which has the following variables (<span style="color: purple;">those continuous refer to millions of USD</span>):
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
1. `investment`: the gross investment, <span style="color: purple;">a continuous response</span>.
2. `market_value`: the firm's market value, <span style="color: purple;">a continuous explanatory variable</span>.
3. `capital`: stock of plant and equipment, <span style="color: purple;">a continuous explanatory variable</span>.
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
4. `firm`: <span style="color: purple;">a nominal explanatory variable</span> with eleven levels indicating the firm (`General Motors`, `US Steel`, `General Electric`, `Chrysler`, `Atlantic Refining`, `IBM`, `Union Oil`, `Westinghouse`, `Goodyear`, `Diamond Match`, and `American Steel`).
5. `year`: the year of the observation (**it will not be used in our analysis**).
:::

### Data in `R`!

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
library(AER)
data(Grunfeld)

Grunfeld <- Grunfeld |> rename(investment = invest, market_value = value)

head(Grunfeld, n = 3)
tail(Grunfeld, n = 3)
```

### iClicker Question

::: {.small-text}

- What class of <span style="color: purple;">data hierarchy</span> do you observe in this dataset? Do you expect any class of <span style="color: purple;">correlation</span> within the data points? **Think about each hierarchical level as a possible sampling pool.**
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
**A.** Yes, we have a data hierarchy with one level: `firm`. Still, there will not be a correlation among subsets of data points.

**B.** Yes, we have a data hierarchy with one level: `firm`. Hence, there will be a correlation among subsets of data points.
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
**C.** There is no data hierarchy at all. All observations in the training set are independent.

**D.** Yes, we have a data hierarchy with two levels: `firm` (<span style="color: purple;">level 1</span>) and the corresponding yearly observations (<span style="color: purple;">level 2</span>). Hence, there will be a correlation among subsets of data points.
:::

### Main Statistical Inquiries

- We are interested in assessing the association of gross `investment` with `market_value` and `capital` <span style="color: purple;">in the population of American firms</span>. 
- Then, how can we fit a linear model to this data?

### 1.2. Exploratory Data Analysis

- Let us plot the 220 data points of `investment` versus `market_value` but <span style="color: purple;">facetted</span> by `firm` and use `geom_smooth()` to fit sub-models by `firm`.

> **Heads-up:** <span style="color: purple;">Only for plotting</span>, we will transform both $x$ and $y$-axes on the logarithmic scale in base 10 (`trans = "log10"`). This allows us to compare those firms under dissimilar market values, capital, and gross investments.

```{r}
#| echo: false
data(Grunfeld)
Grunfeld <- Grunfeld |> rename(investment = invest, market_value = value)

scatterplots_firm_market_value <- Grunfeld |>
  ggplot(aes(market_value, investment)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", fullrange = TRUE, formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~firm) +
  labs(x = "Market Value \n (Millions of American Dollars on a Log Scale in Base 10)", 
       y = "Gross Investment \n (Millions of American Dollars on a Log Scale in Base 10)") +
  ggtitle("Scatterplots by Firm of Market Value versus Gross Investments") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 25, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 22),
    strip.text.x = element_text(size = 22),
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10") +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "log10")

scatterplots_firm_capital <- Grunfeld |>
  ggplot(aes(capital, investment)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", fullrange = TRUE, formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~firm) +
  labs(x = "Capital \n (Millions of American Dollars on a Log Scale in Base 10)", 
       y = "Gross Investment \n (Millions of American Dollars on a Log Scale in Base 10)") +
  ggtitle("Scatterplots by Firm of Capital versus Gross Investments") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 25, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 22),
    strip.text.x = element_text(size = 22),
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10") +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "log10")
```


### Plots!

```{r}
#| fig.width: 20
#| fig.height: 10
scatterplots_firm_market_value
```

### 1.3. OLS General Modelling Framework

- Before digging into today's new modelling approach, let us try a <span style="color: purple;">classical approach</span> via Ordinary Least-squares (OLS) for <span style="color: purple;">comparative purposes</span>.

> **Heads-up:** Always keep in mind the main statistical inquiry when taking any given modelling approach.

####  1.3.1. Regression Alternatives

- Based on what we have seen via OLS in <span style="color: purple;">DSCI 561</span>, there might be four possible approaches:

::: {.incremental}
1. Take the average for each `firm`, and fit an ordinary least-squares (OLS) regression on the averages. <span style="color: purple;">This is not an ideal approach</span>.
2. <span style="color: purple;">We could ignore `firm`</span>. <span style="color: purple;">This is not an ideal approach</span>.
3. <span style="color: purple;">Allow different intercepts for each `firm`.</span>
4. <span style="color: purple;">Allow a different slope and intercept for each `firm`</span> (i.e., an <span style="color: purple;">interaction model</span>!).
:::

#### 1.3.2. OLS Ignoring Firm

<br>

- Let us start with this basic OLS model to warm up our modelling skills regarding setting up equations.
- The regression equation for the $i$th sampled observation will be:

. . .

::: {.small-text}
\begin{align*}
\texttt{investment}_{i} &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \texttt{marketValue}_{i} + \beta_2\texttt{capital}_{i} + \varepsilon_{i} \\
& \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{for} \; i = 1, \ldots, 220.
\end{align*}
:::

#### Code in `R!`

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
ordinary_model <- lm(formula = investment ~ market_value + capital, data = Grunfeld)
tidy(ordinary_model) |>
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 4)
glance(ordinary_model) |>
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 4)
```

#### 1.3.3. OLS Regression with Varying Intercept

:::: {.small-text}
::: {.incremental}
- Let us estimate another OLS model with `investment` as a response to `market_value` and `capital` as regressors <span style="color: purple;">but with varying intercepts by each `firm`</span>.
- We can use `lm()` by adding `- 1` on the right-hand side of the argument `formula`.
- This `- 1` will allow the baseline `firm` to have its intercept (i.e., renaming `(Intercept)` in column `estimate` with `firmCompanyName`).
:::
::::

. . .

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
levels(Grunfeld$firm)
```

#### Fitting model in `R`!

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
model_varying_intercept <- lm(
  formula = investment ~ market_value + capital + firm - 1, data = Grunfeld
)
tidy(model_varying_intercept) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 4)
```

#### Glancing model in `R`!

<br>

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
glance(model_varying_intercept) |>
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 4) 
```

#### Model Comparison

- By checking the `adj.r.squared`, we see that `model_varying_intercept` has a larger value (**0.959**) than `ordinary_model` (**0.816**).
- Note that `model_varying_intercept` is equivalent to just fitting the OLS model using:

`formula = investment ~ market_value + capital + firm`.

. . .

- Let us check the above fact!

#### Using `lm()` without `-1`

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
primary_OLS <- lm(investment ~ market_value + capital + firm , data = Grunfeld)
tidy(primary_OLS) |>
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 4) 
```

#### $F$-test

::: {.small-text}
- Going back to `model_varying_intercept` and `ordinary_model`, we can test if there is a gain in considering a varying intercept versus fixed intercept. 
- Hence, we will make a formal $F$-test <span style="color: purple;">to check whether the `model_varying_intercept` fits the data better than the `ordinary_model`</span>.
:::

. . .

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
anova(ordinary_model, model_varying_intercept) |>
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 4) 
```

#### Testing Conclusion 

::: {.small-text}
- We obtain a $p\text{-value} < .001$. 
- Thus, with $\alpha = 0.05$, we have evidence to conclude that `model_varying_intercept` fits the data better than the `ordinary_model`.
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
- However, this costs us one extra degree of freedom per `firm` <span style="color: purple;">except for the baseline</span>. 
- Therefore, we lose another 10 <span style="color: purple;">degrees of freedom</span> (column `DF` in the `anova()` output).
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}

> **Heads-up:** In this specific case, losing 10 degrees of freedom is not a big deal with 220 data points. Nonetheless, **when data is scarce or the model's complexity demands a large amount of regression parameters**, this could be an issue.

:::

\begin{align*}

& \qquad \qquad \quad \text{for} \; i = 1, \ldots, 20 \; \; \text{and} \; \; j = 1, \ldots, 11.
\end{align*}
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
**B.**
\begin{align*}
\texttt{investment}_{i} &= \beta_{0} + \beta_1 \texttt{marketValue}_{i} + \beta_2\texttt{capital}_{i} + \varepsilon_{i} \\
& \qquad \qquad \quad \text{for} \; i = 1, \ldots, 220.
\end{align*}
:::

\begin{align*}
\texttt{investment}_{i,j} &= \beta_{0,j} + \beta_1 \texttt{marketValue}_{i,j} + \beta_2\texttt{capital}_{i,j} + \varepsilon_{i,j} \\
& \qquad \qquad \quad \text{for} \; i = 1, \ldots, 20 \; \; \text{and} \; \; j = 1, \ldots, 11.

### 1.3.4. OLS Regression for Each Firm

- We fit a more complex OLS model with <span style="color: purple;">two interactions</span>.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
model_by_firm <- lm(investment ~ market_value * firm + capital * firm, data = Grunfeld)
tidy(model_by_firm) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 2)
```

#### Glancing model in `R`!

<br>

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
glance(model_by_firm) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 2)
```

#### A note on this model!

<br>

- In this case, we are fitting eleven linear regressions, each with 20 points.

. . .

> **Heads-up:** We have <span style="color: purple;">plenty of data points</span> in this case <span style="color: purple;">for all the degrees of freedom</span> required to estimate each parameter. Nonetheless, this might not hold for other small datasets. Also, we must consider other modelling scenarios in which there may be more than two regressors of interest with different natures (discrete and continuous), which may require a <span style="color: purple;">large number of degrees of freedom</span>.

#### iClicker Question

::: {.small-text}
What is the sample's regression equation for `model_by_firm`?

**A.**

\begin{align*}
\texttt{investment}_{i,j} &= \beta_{0,j} + \beta_{1,j} \texttt{marketValue}_{i,j} + \beta_{2,j} \texttt{capital}_{i,j} + \varepsilon_{i,j} \\
& \qquad \qquad \quad \text{for} \; i = 1, \ldots, 20 \; \; \text{and} \; \; j = 1, \ldots, 11.
\end{align*}

**B.**

\begin{align*}
\texttt{investment}_{j} &= \beta_{0} + \beta_1 \texttt{marketValue}_{j} + \beta_2\texttt{capital}_{j} + \varepsilon_{j} \\
& \qquad \qquad \quad \text{for} \; j = 1, \ldots, 11.
\end{align*}

**C.**
\begin{align*}
\texttt{investment}_{i,j} &= \beta_{0,i} + \beta_{1,i} \texttt{marketValue}_{i,j} + \beta_{2,i} \texttt{capital}_{i,j} + \varepsilon_{i,j} \\
& \qquad \qquad \quad \text{for} \; i = 1, \ldots, 20 \; \; \text{and} \; \; j = 1, \ldots, 11.
\end{align*}
:::

#### How to interpret the coefficients in this model?

::: {.small-text}
> Each regression coefficient is associated with a `firm`. For example, $\texttt{firmUS Steel:capital} = 0.02$ means that the variable `capital` has a slope of $0.02 + 0.37 = 0.39$ for `US Steel`. We can double-check this by estimating an individual linear regression for `US Steel`.
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
tidy(lm(investment ~ market_value + capital, data = Grunfeld |>
  filter(firm == "US Steel"))) |>
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 2)
```

## 2. Linear Mixed-effects Model

- Let us take a step back and think about a <span style="color: purple;">population of companies</span>. For instance, <span style="color: purple;">all American companies</span>.

. . .

- Grunfeld did not collect data on all the American companies but sampled 11 companies from this population. The author was interested in assessing whether `market_value` and `capital` were related to `investment` and by how much.

### Mixed Intercept!

- Let us assume that the $j$th sampled `firm` has its own intercept $b_{0,j}$ and the <span style="color: purple;">overall fixed intercept</span> is $\beta_0$ <span style="color: purple;">for all American companies</span>. 
- Therefore, for the $j$th firm we define the following <span style="color: purple;">mixed</span> intercept:

. . .

\begin{equation*}
\beta_{0,j} = \beta_0 + b_{0,j}.
\end{equation*}

- Term $b_{0,j}$ will change due to chance since it is linked the $j$th sampled `firm` which would make it a <span style="color: purple;">random effect</span>.

### Changing our Regression Paradigm!

:::{.small-text}
- The <span style="color: purple;">regression paradigm</span> of estimating a fixed unknown intercept $\beta_0$ will change now. Moreover, the intercept $\beta_{0,j}$ is what we call a <span style="color: purple;">mixed effect</span>.

\begin{align*}
\texttt{investment}_{i,j} &= \overbrace{\beta_{0,j}}^{\text{Mixed Effect}} + \beta_1 \texttt{marketValue}_{i,j} + \\
& \qquad \quad \beta_2\texttt{capital}_{i,j} + \varepsilon_{i,j} \\
&=  (\beta_0 + b_{0,j}) + \beta_1 \texttt{marketValue}_{i,j} + \\
& \qquad \quad \beta_2\texttt{capital}_{i,j} + \varepsilon_{i,j} \\ & \qquad \qquad \; \; \; \; \text{for} \; i = 1, \ldots, n_j \; \; \text{and} \; \; j = 1, \ldots, 11.
\end{align*}

> **Heads-up:** Note that $n_j$ is making the model even more flexible by allowing different numbers of observations $n_j$ in each $j$th firm.
:::

### Now...

$$b_{0,j}\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_0^2)$$ 

is called a <span style="color: purple;">random effect</span> and we assume it is independent of the error component 

$$\varepsilon_{i,j}\sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2).$$

> **Heads-up:** The observations for the same `firm` (group) share the same random effect <span style="color: purple;">making a correlation structure</span>.

### And the variance is...

- The variance of the $i$th response for the $j$th `firm` will be
\begin{equation*}
\text{Var}(\texttt{investment}_{i,j}) = Var(b_{0,j}) + Var(\varepsilon_{i,j}) = \sigma_0^2 + \sigma^2.
\end{equation*}

- For the $k$th and $l$th responses, within the $j$th firm, the <span style="color: purple;">correlation</span> is given by:
\begin{equation*}
\text{Corr}(\texttt{investment}_{k,j}, \texttt{investment}_{l,j}) = \frac{\sigma^2_0}{\sigma_0^2 + \sigma^2}.
\end{equation*}

### Random Slopes!

. . .

:::{.small-text}
- We could even go further and model random slopes, along with the existing fixed ones, as follows:
\begin{align*}
\texttt{investment}_{i,j}
&= \overbrace{\beta_{0,j}}^{\text{Mixed Effect}} + \overbrace{\beta_{1,j}}^{\text{Mixed Effect}} \times \texttt{marketValue}_{i,j} + \\
& \qquad \quad \overbrace{\beta_{2,j}}^{\text{Mixed Effect}} \times \texttt{capital}_{i,j} + \varepsilon_{i,j} \\
&=  (\beta_0 + b_{0,j}) + (\beta_1 + b_{1,j}) \times \texttt{marketValue}_{i,j} + \\
& \qquad \quad (\beta_2 + b_{2,j}) \times \texttt{capital}_{i,j} + \varepsilon_{i,j} \\
& \qquad \qquad \qquad \text{for} \; i = 1, \ldots, n_j \; \; \text{and} \; \; j = 1, \ldots, 11;
\end{align*}

- Note $(b_{0,j}, b_{1,j}, b_{2,j})^{T} \sim \mathcal{N}_3(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{D})$, where $\mathbf{0} = (0, 0, 0)^T$ and $\mathbf{D}$ is a <span style="color: purple;">generic covariance matrix</span>.
:::

### 2.1. What is this Generic Covariance Matrix $\mathbf{D}$?

- This is a <span style="color: purple;">standard form</span> in linear mixed effects modelling. 
- Hence, this matrix becomes:

\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{D} =
\begin{bmatrix}
\sigma_{0}^2 & \rho_{01} \sigma_{0} \sigma_{1} & \rho_{02} \sigma_{0} \sigma_{2}\\
\rho_{01} \sigma_{0} \sigma_{1} & \sigma_{1}^2 & \rho_{12} \sigma_{1} \sigma_{2}\\
\rho_{02} \sigma_{0} \sigma_{2} & \rho_{12} \sigma_{1} \sigma_{2} & \sigma_{2}^2
\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}
\sigma_{0}^2 & \sigma_{0, 1} & \sigma_{0, 2} \\
\sigma_{0, 1} & \sigma_{1}^2 & \sigma_{1,2}\\
\sigma_{0, 2} & \sigma_{1, 2}  & \sigma_{2}^2
\end{bmatrix}
\end{equation*}

### Important Notes

- The joint Normal distribution explains the variability of <span style="color: purple;">random</span> regression coefficients and intercepts. The spread does not change when we collect more data.
- The <span style="color: purple;">sampling distribution</span> explains the uncertainty in the <span style="color: purple;">fixed</span> regression estimates and <span style="color: purple;">gets narrower</span> as we collect more data.

### 2.2. Model Fitting, Inference, and Coefficient Interpretation

- Let us estimate the regression model with a mixed intercept only (`mixed_intercept_model`) via the function `lmer()` from package `lme4`. 
- Note that `(1 | firm)` allows the model to have a random intercept by `firm`.

<center>        
<img src="images/bulb.png" width="180" height="225"/>
</center>

---

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| warning: false
mixed_intercept_model <- lmer(
  investment ~ market_value +
    capital + (1 | firm),
  data = Grunfeld
)
print(mixed_intercept_model)
```

#### Estimate the Mixed-effects

<br>

- Now, let us estimate the Mixed-effects regression model with <span style="color: purple;">mixed intercept and slopes</span> (`full_mixed_model`).

<center>        
<img src="images/bulb.png" width="180" height="225"/>
</center>

---

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| warning: false
full_mixed_model <- lmer(
  investment ~ market_value +
    capital + (market_value + capital | firm),
  data = Grunfeld
)
print(full_mixed_model)
```

#### Inference

- Let us proceed with inference using `mixed_intercept_model`. 
- We now assess whether the fixed effects are <span style="color: purple;">statistically associated</span> with `investment` in each model via `summary()`. 
- We will use the package `lmerTest` via function `summary()`.

<center>        
<img src="images/bulb.png" width="135" height="168.75"/>
</center>

---

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
library(lmerTest)
summary(mixed_intercept_model)
```

---

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
summary(full_mixed_model)
```

#### Inferential Conclusion

<br>

- We can see that `market_value` and `capital` are significant with $\alpha = 0.05$ in both models. 
- Moreover, the <span style="color: purple;">regression coefficients' interpretation</span> for the fixed effects will be on the effect these regressors have on the population `investment` mean of the American companies. 
- We can obtain the estimated coefficients by `firm` along with the intercepts for both models via `coef()`.

#### Getting coefficients in `R`!

<br>

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
coef(mixed_intercept_model)$firm
```

---

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
coef(full_mixed_model)$firm
```

#### Some notes!

::: {.small-text}
- Column `(Intercept)` is the <span style="color: purple;">sum</span> $\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{b}_{0,j}$. 
- Note the estimated regression coefficients for `market_value` and `capital` are the <span style="color: purple;">same</span> since `mixed_intercept_model` only has $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ as its general modelling setup.
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
- The coefficient summary changes in `full_mixed_model` given that <span style="color: purple;">we also include random effects</span> for `market_value` and `capital`.
- Columns `market_value` and `capital` are the <span style="color: purple;">sums</span> $\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{b}_{1,j}$ and $\hat{\beta}_2 + \hat{b}_{2,j}$, respectively. 
- Column `(Intercept)` is the <span style="color: purple;">sum</span> $\hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{b}_{0,j}$.
:::

#### In-class Question

- Note the standard errors for the estimated slopes in `market_value` and `capital` behave in a really particular way when comparing the OLS `model_varying_intercept` and the Mixed-effects `full_mixed_model`.
- Therefore, **what are the advantages of a Mixed-effects model over an OLS model with fixed-effects only?**

<center>        
<img src="images/panda.png" width="175" height="175"/>
</center>

---

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
tidy(model_varying_intercept) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 4)
```

---

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
summary(full_mixed_model)
```

### 2.3. Estimation

- Mixed-effects models are still fit using <span style="color: purple;">likelihood</span> ideas.
- Compared to OLS, there is *more* to estimate:
  - **Fixed effects:** intercept and coefficients.
  - **Overall variance:** $\sigma^2$.
  - **Variance components (associated to random effects):** how much groups/subjects vary (and sometimes how random effects move together).

#### REML: Restricted Maximum Likelihood

- **REML** is a <span style="color: purple;">common estimation approach</span> for Mixed-effects regression.

. . .

- **Intuition:** estimating fixed effects “*uses up*” information, so <span style="color: purple;">plain maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)</span> can **underestimate** random-effect variances.
- REML focuses on <span style="color: purple;">variation left over after accounting for fixed effects</span>.

#### Two Steps in Practice

1. Estimate <span style="color: purple;">variance components</span> (random-effect variances/covariances and $\sigma^2$).
2. Estimate <span style="color: purple;">fixed effects</span> given those variance estimates (a weighted regression accounting for within-group correlation).

<center>        
<img src="images/panda.png" width="250" height="250"/>
</center>

### 2.4. Prediction

We can make two classes of predictions with Mixed-effects models:

1. <span style="color: purple;">To predict on an existing group</span>, we find that group's regression coefficients (and therefore model function) by summing the fixed effects and (if present) the random effects, then use that model function to make predictions.

. . .

2. <span style="color: purple;">To predict on a new group (using a mean prediction)</span>, we use the fixed effects as the regression coefficients (because the random effects have mean zero) and use that model function to make predictions. 

#### Code in `R`!

::: {.small-text}
- For <span style="color: purple;">predictions on an existing group in our training set</span> we have:
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
round(predict(full_mixed_model, newdata = tibble(
  firm = "General Motors",
  market_value = 2000, capital = 1000
)), 2)
```

. . .

::: {.small-text}
> If we wanted <span style="color: purple;">to predict the `investment` for `General Motors`</span> with a `market_value` of USD $\$2,000$ million and capital of USD $\$1,000$ million, then our answer would be USD $\$537.4$ million. 

- This prediction uses $\hat{\beta}_0$, $\hat{\beta}_1$, $\hat{\beta}_2$, $\hat{b}_{0, j}$, $\hat{b}_{1, j}$, and $\hat{b}_{2, j}$.
:::

#### Make prediction for new observations!

<br>

::: {.small-text}
- For <span style="color: purple;">predictions on American companies in general</span>, we have:
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
newdata <- tibble(firm = "New Company", market_value = 2000, capital = 1000)
prdct <- predict(full_mixed_model, newdata, allow.new.levels = TRUE)
round(prdct, 2)
```

. . .

::: {.small-text}
> If we wanted <span style="color: purple;">to predict the MEAN `investment` for American companies</span> with a `market_value` of USD $\$2,000$ million and capital of USD $\$1,000$ million, then our answer would be USD $\$341.51$ million. This prediction only uses $\hat{\beta_0}$, $\hat{\beta_1}$, and $\hat{\beta_2}$.
:::

## 3. Wrapping Up

- In many different cases, when there is a <span style="color: purple;">correlation structure</span> in our observations, OLS models are not suitable for our inferential or predictive inquiries.
- Therefore, <span style="color: purple;">linear Mixed-effects models </span> are suitable for correlated observations. 
- Nonetheless, the model's complexity will also be in function of our specific inquiries.
- We can even extend the Mixed-effects approach to generalized linear models (GLMs)!
